evidence.title: Human Factors Validation Study of an Artificial Neural Network‑based Preoperative Decision‑support Tool for Noninvasive Lymph Node Staging (NILS) in Women with Primary Breast Cancer (ISRCTN99301435)
evidence.outcome: Usability problems and use errors found in simulated-case testing with representative physician users
evidence.effect: Mean SUS 89.5 and ASQ 6.3/7; testing still uncovered interface problems (hard-to-find reset/info buttons, out-of-range entry, accidental value changes while scrolling), prompting ongoing redesign.
evidence.quote: Several interface challenges were identified, including difficulty in locating the reset and information buttons, the ability to enter values outside valid ranges (age and tumor size), and the risk of unintentionally modifying the entered values while scrolling.

evidence.title: User-centred design of a clinical decision support system for palliative care: Insights from healthcare professionals
evidence.outcome: Whether usability testing with potential users identified workflow implementation issues
evidence.effect: Think-aloud and UX assessment identified most workflow implementation issues; SUS 62.7±14.1 and 65±26.2 in two rounds; UEQ-S 1.42 and 1.5.
evidence.quote: The think-aloud method and including the UX dimension helped us to identify most of the workflow implementation issues.

evidence.title: Comparing ChatGPT-4 and Human Translation of an Outcome Questionnaire: A Randomized, Double-Blinded Non-inferiority Study
evidence.effect: Conducting face validation with representative patients allowed correction of the AI's shortcomings, eliminating significant differences in understandability compared to human translation.
evidence.quote: However, the lack of significant differences after face validation implies that ChatGPT-4’s shortcomings were corrected through the face validation process.

evidence.title: AI-Based Gait Analysis System for Rehabilitation: Usability Evaluation of Human-Technology Interaction
evidence.outcome: System usability (SUS) and usability barriers found in scenario-based testing with end users
evidence.effect: Mean SUS score 57 (grade D), suboptimal usability. Testing with 5 physical therapists surfaced barriers: power button access, no battery indicator, burdensome manual calibration, insufficient report detail.
evidence.quote: The mean SUS score was 57 (grade D), indicating suboptimal usability and the need for iterative design refinements.

evidence.title: The Illusion of Understanding: A Randomized Controlled Trial of LLM-Generated Lay Summaries of Brain MRI Reports
evidence.outcome: Gap between perceived and actual understanding of AI-generated outputs among patients
evidence.effect: Subjective comprehension rose (50.3% vs 24.0%; OR 3.17) while objective comprehension did not change (58.3% vs 59.4%); normal reports had reduced comprehension (72.5% vs 76.6%).
evidence.quote: LLM-generated lay summaries appended to brain MRI reports improved patient satisfaction and subjective comprehension but did not improve objective comprehension, indicating a gap between perceived and actual understanding that should be addressed before clinical integration.

evidence.title: Testing a Novel Design Framework for Patient-Facing Machine Learning-Based Predictions of Heart Failure Decompensation
evidence.outcome: Patient comprehension of predictive algorithm output, threshold, and contributing sensors in prototype usability testing
evidence.effect: Comprehension of output 80% to 85%; threshold comprehension 60% to 85%; comprehension of contributing CIED sensors 63% to 93% (n=20).
evidence.quote: Comprehension of the algorithm output was high across conditions (80% to 85%), but comprehension of the algorithm's threshold varied (60% to 85%), as did comprehension of the CIED sensors contributing to the algorithm (63% to 93%).

evidence.title: Optimizing AI implementation for surgery: recommendations for infrastructure and deployment in the operating room
evidence.outcome: Deployment task completion and interface usability issues with representative end users
evidence.effect: Task completion median 100% Cloud vs 80% Edge (p=2.16×10−5). SUS 65.33 vs 69.67, not significant. Most frequent Edge improvement suggestions concerned the interface (16).
evidence.quote: Participants achieved a higher completion rate for AI deployment tasks when using Cloud (median 100%, IQR 100–100%) compared to Edge (median 80%, IQR 80–80%).

commentary.bottom_line: Four simulated studies, three of which enrolled 5 to 20 participants, suggest that usability testing with representative users finds interface problems and comprehension gaps before deployment, but none measured whether testing reduced use errors or patient harm in live care. Frameworks, FDA draft guidance, and commentaries endorse the practice, while certainty that it prevents incorrect actions is very low.

perspectives.view: All four tests are level 4 studies in offline or simulated settings. Three enrolled 5 to 20 participants, and one did not report its sample size. Their outcomes were problems detected or usability scores, which measure correct action only indirectly. The one randomized design enrolled 20 patients. Serious imprecision and indirectness support a rating of very low certainty.

Testing surfaced use errors such as out-of-range entry and accidental value changes while scrolling, even with a mean SUS of 89.5. In a French trial of 2,727 participants, subjective comprehension rose (50.3% vs 24.0%) while objective comprehension did not change (58.3% vs 59.4%). This suggests testing should measure actual understanding rather than satisfaction.

Think-aloud testing identified most workflow implementation issues in one study, and scenario testing with 5 physical therapists found calibration and reporting barriers. In a clinician vignette study, median task completion differed (100% vs 80%) while SUS did not, which suggests task completion may detect problems that satisfaction scores miss.

One test involved non-English-speaking patients in Denmark and found that face validation corrected AI translation shortcomings, eliminating significant differences in understandability compared with human translation. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users, so the evidence does not show whether testing detects comprehension failures in those groups.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to analyze whether a device has tasks where use errors could cause harm, and a regulator discussion paper lists communication quality and user comprehension as a topic. No supplied study tested whether this kind of human factors validation changes outcomes after deployment.

Three studies reported samples of 5 to 23 participants in simulated sessions, which suggests pre-deployment testing can surface interface problems with modest samples. None reported cost, staff time, or how often retesting was needed after model or interface updates, so the resources required at scale remain unknown.

In prototype testing with 20 patients, comprehension of an algorithm's threshold ranged from 60% to 85%. Patients who felt they understood AI reports did not understand them better on objective measures. These findings suggest that including patients in testing may reveal misunderstanding before outputs reach them in care.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested whether usability testing before deployment reduced use errors, incorrect clinical actions, or patient harm in live care. Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without structured human factors validation, measure objective comprehension of outputs and uncertainty, report the staff time and cost of testing, and enroll Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy users.
commentary.underserved_note: One test included limited English proficiency or non-English-speaking patients, in a 20-patient Danish study of AI translation. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so it is unknown whether representative-user testing detects comprehension failures among those users.
